scenario.fault_family: link cut (backbone redundancy loss, traffic rerouted)
scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8880: NOC monitoring reports that the OSPF adjacency between
router_core_1 and router_core_3 dropped a few minutes ago and has not come
back. There are no user complaints: both pods still reach the server farm
normally, and all portals load. We are concerned the backbone is now running
without redundancy on pod 1's path to the data center. Confirm what failed
and exactly where, so the right link can be repaired.

injection.action: bring down the backbone link to router_core_3

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth1 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router_core_1's eth1 interface -- the
  router_core_1<->router_core_3 backbone link (172.16.0.2/31, area 0)
Mechanism: the core is a triangle (core1-core2, core1-core3, core2-core3).
  router_core_1's eth1 (172.16.0.2/31, the direct link to router_core_3) is
  administratively DOWN, so the adjacency to neighbor 172.16.0.3 dropped
  immediately. OSPF reconverges around the failure: pod-1 traffic to the
  server farm now flows router_core_1 -> router_core_2 -> router_core_3, so
  end-to-end connectivity is preserved and users see nothing. The observable
  fault is the lost adjacency and the down interface -- the backbone has
  lost its redundancy, not its reachability. Note the asymmetry evidence:
  router_core_3's own eth0 still shows UP (only router_core_1's side of the
  link was taken down), which localizes the failure to router_core_1's end.
Localization: router_core_1 eth1 (the 172.16.0.2/31 link to router_core_3)
Root cause: backbone link router_core_1<->router_core_3 down
  (router_core_1's eth1 administratively down)
Fix: `ip link set eth1 up` on router_core_1
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth1 up` on router_core_1

agent.diagnosis_text: The affected component is the OSPF adjacency on the core backhaul between router_core_1 and router_core_3. The failure is at Layer 1 on router_core_1’s eth1 interface, which carries the point-to-point /31 link to router_core_3 eth0. On router_core_1, ethtool shows Link detected: no on eth1 and ip -br confirms eth1 is DOWN with 172.16.0.2/31. OSPF neighbors on router_core_1 list only the peers on eth0 and eth2; there is no neighbor on eth1, confirming the adjacency is down on that side. On router_core_3, eth0 is UP/LOWER_UP with 172.16.0.3/31, but a direct ping sourced from eth0 to 172.16.0.2 returns Destination Host Unreachable, demonstrating the far end is not present even though the local interface remains electrically up. Mechanistically, loss of carrier on router_core_1 eth1 stops OSPF hellos, so the adjacency to router_core_3 drops. Traffic remains unaffected because OSPF has converged to the alternate path via router_core_2 (r1–r2–r3), preserving reachability to the server farm but eliminating redundancy on pod 1’s path. Root cause: physical link/cable or port failure on router_core_1 eth1 for the r1:eth1 ↔ r3:eth0 interconnect. Corrective fix: dispatch to repair/replace the patch or optics on router_core_1 eth1 (and reseat/check the port), then bring the interface back; OSPF will reestablish automatically once carrier returns.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly identifies the router_core_1 ↔ router_core_3 backbone link and cites router_core_1 eth1 with 172.16.0.2/31 as the failed/adjacency-lost link.

The agent's logs clearly show router_core_1 eth1 is DOWN while router_core_3 eth0 is UP, OSPF adjacency is missing from r1 and pings to the far address fail — supporting the adjacency/localization claim. The agent infers a Layer-1 problem causing the adjacency loss (logical), but attributes it specifically to a physical/cable fault rather than an administrative shutdown without direct proof.
